div.p: In uniform multiprocessor platforms, the various processors comprising the multiprocessor platform may have different computing capacities. The focus of this paper is the design of efficient tests for determining whether the Earliest Deadline First Scheduling Algorithm (EDF) can successfully schedule a given real-time task system to meet all deadlines upon a specified uniform multiprocessor platform. Upon uniform multiprocessor platforms, we show that it is often far easier (from a computational complexity perspective) to determine feasibility than it is to check for EDF-schedulability.

In designing an EDF-schedulability test for uniform multiprocessors, therefore, our approach is as follows: for a given uniform multiprocessor platform, we attempt to efficiently identify all those uniform multiprocessor platforms such that any real-time instance feasible upon these platforms is guaranteed to be EDF-schedulable upon the platform under consideration. EDF-schedulability upon the given platform can then be determined by ascertaining whether the real-time system is feasible upon any of these platforms.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: While real-time scheduling upon uniprocessor platforms has been extensively studied, it is only recently that multiprocessor real-time scheduling has attracted much attention. In this paper, we consider the scheduling of real-time task systems upon uniform multiprocessors -multiprocessor platforms in which all processors are not required to be identical to one another.

The Earliest Deadline First scheduling algorithm (EDF) [9,3] is a very popular real-time scheduling algorithm that has been extensively studied for both uniprocessors and multiprocessors. While EDF has been shown [9,3] to be optimal on uniprocessors, it is known [6,4] that no on-line scheduling algorithm can be optimal upon multiprocessors. Despite this lack of optimality, EDF possesses many additional desirable properties that make it an attractive algorithm to use in scheduling multiprocessor real-time systems. efficient tests for determining whether EDF can successfully schedule a given real-time task system to meet all deadlines upon a specified uniform multiprocessor platform.

A collection Á of real-time jobs (in this paper, we will often refer to such collections as real-time instances) is said to be feasible upon a processor platform if there is some schedule for Á upon that will result in all deadlines of Á being met. For any scheduling algorithm , Á is defined to beschedulable upon if will schedule Á upon to meet all deadlines. Upon uniform multiprocessor platforms, it turns out that it is often far easier (from a computational complexity perspective) to determine feasibility than it is to check for EDF-schedulability (see Example 5 in Section 3 for an example of this phenomenon). In designing an EDF-schedulability test for uniform multiprocessors, therefore, our approach is as follows: for a given uniform multiprocessor platform , we will derive an efficient algorithm to identify all those uniform multiprocessor platforms ¼ such that any real-time instance feasible upon ¼ is guaranteed to be EDF-schedulable upon . To do so, we find it convenient to group uniform multiprocessors into classes: A uniform multiprocessor ¼ belongs to the class ©´ µ if its fastest processor has speed and its total processor speed is . The set of all such classes is denoted . For each multiprocessor , the characteristic region ( Ê ) of is the subset of that satisfies the following property: If ´ µ ¾ Ê and Á is a real-time instance that is known to be feasible on a uniform multiprocessor ¼ ¾ ©´ µ, then Á is guaranteed to be EDF-schedulable on . Moreover, if ´ µ ¾ Ê there exists some uniform multiprocessor ¼ ¾ ©´ µ and some set of jobs Á such that Á is feasible on ¼ but not EDF-schedulable on . Thus, Ê completely defines the region for which feasibility on a multiprocessor within the region guarantees EDFschedulability on . To demonstrate that a given instance Á is EDF-schedulable upon , it therefore suffices to identify some platform ¼ whose class is in Ê , and upon which Á is feasible; as stated above, feasibility-analysis is often an easier problem than EDF-schedulability analysis upon uniform multiprocessors (particularly when one has some choice in determining the precise characteristics of the platform ¼ ).

The remainder of this paper is arranged as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the models and definitions that we will use in subsequent sections. In Section 3, we discuss previous results that pertain to the work introduced in this paper. In Section 4, we describe an Ç´Ñµ method for finding points in Ê . Finally, in Section 5 we provide concluding remarks and outline future work in this area.

div.head: Models and Definitions
div.p: A real-time instance, Á ½ ¾ Ò , is a (possibly infinite) collection of time-constrained jobs. Each job ¾ Á is completely defined by the 3-tuple ´ µ, where is the job's arrival time, is its worst-case execution requirement, and its deadline. A real-time system is a realtime instance paired with a specific computer processing platform. The platform may be a uniprocessor, consisting of one processor, or it may be a multiprocessor, consisting of several processors. If the platform is a multiprocessor, the individual processors may all be the same or they may differ from one another. Much of the research concerning real-time scheduling on multiprocessors considers identical multiprocessors, in which all processors execute at the same speed. However, other types of multiprocessors, such as uniform multiprocessors, have also been considered [10,11,7]. On these platforms, each processor has an associated speed: if a job executes on a processor with speed × for one unit of time, the processor will perform × units of work. Notice that identical multiprocessors are a special case of uniform multiprocessors. Therefore, the results found in this paper also apply to identical multiprocessors.
The following notation is used to describe uniform multiprocessors.

Given a real-time system, a scheduling algorithm is used to determine which jobs get scheduled at each point in time.

A real-time instance Á is called feasible on a computing platform if there exists some scheduling algorithm for which each job ¾ Á receives units of execution in the time interval µ. If an instance Á is feasible on a multiprocessor platform and A is an algorithm that schedules Á to meet all its deadlines, then Á is called A-schedulable on . One popular scheduling algorithm is Earliest Deadline First (EDF), which satisfies the following properties when implemented on an Ñ-processor uniform multiprocessor.
¯When more than Ñ jobs are ready for execution, the Ñ jobs with the earliest deadlines must be selected for execution.
¯A job can never execute on more than one processor at any point in time.
¯A processor idles only if no jobs are waiting to execute.
¯Jobs with earlier deadlines are always assigned to faster processors.
¯Idling processors are never faster than processors that are executing jobs.

Notice that the final two specifications imply that jobs may migrate form one processor to another. EDF is a well-known and efficient scheduling algorithm. In this paper, we provide a test that can be used to discern if an instance Á will meet all its deadlines using EDF on a given multiprocessor . The central point of this test is consideration of 's characteristic region -if an instance Á is feasible on some multiprocessor ¼ in this region, then Á is guaranteed to be EDF-schedulable on . For every Ñ-processor uniform multiprocessor , this paper introduces an Ç´Ñµ-time method for dividing the space of classes of uniform multiprocessor, , into three distinct regions: classes that are known to be in Ê , classes that are known to be outside of Ê , and classes whose membership in Ê is currently undetermined. In many cases, the third class can be shown to be empty and the region Ê can be completely determined in Ç´Ñµ time.

div.head: The Characteristic Region of
div.p: For every Ñ-processor uniform multiprocessor , methods introduced in this section divide the space of classes of uniform multiprocessors into three regions, all of which can be efficiently identified in Ç´Ñµ time. The first region contains the classes of multiprocessors that are proven to be in Ê . If Á is feasible on any multiprocessor that falls within this region, then Á is EDF-schedulable on . The second region contains classes of multiprocessors that are definitely not in Ê . For every ´ µ in this region, we find a real-time instance Á that is feasible on some uniform multiprocessor ¼ ¾ ©´ µ but is not EDF-schedulable on . Finally, we

have not yet determined whether multiprocessors in the third region are in Ê or not, though we conjecture that all points in this region are not in Ê . There are many multiprocessors for which this third region is empty. If this third region is empty for a given multiprocessor then the critical region is fully determined by methods introduced in this paper. In particular, we will show that the critical region can be completely determined for every identical multiprocessor.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: EDF is a very popular and efficient scheduling algorithm. The results presented in this paper allow EDF to be used on a new type of platform with confidence that all deadlines will be met. EDF-schedulability on a processing platform is determined by considering feasibility on a less powerful platform ¼ . In many cases, feasibility is easier to determine than schedulability using a specific scheduling algorithm. Therefore, this paper takes the difficult question of whether EDF can be used to schedule a real-time instance Á on and reduces it to the relatively easier question of whether any scheduling algorithm can be used to schedule Á on a different (less powerful) platform ¼ .

A central concept of this paper is the development of a characteristic region, Ê . The region contains classes of uniform multiprocessors -any real-time instance feasible on some multiprocessor within one of these classes will be EDFschedulable on . In Ç´Ñµ time, one can divide all classes of uniform multiprocessors into three regions: those that are definitely in Ê , those that are definitely not in Ê , and those whose membership in Ê is currently not determined. Moreover, in many cases the third region is empty. In the future, we hope to fully determine the shape of Ê for all uniform multiprocessors. We conjecture that Ê contains only those points that we have already proven to be in Ê (i.e., we believe Ê Ö ).
